issues.legal_issue: A trial court may add or alter a criminal charge at any time before judgment when relevant material supports the proposed charge, subject to safeguards against prejudice to a fair trial.
material_facts: An additional charge-sheet and an order taking cognizance of further offences were in the trial court record, but the additional charge-sheet was overlooked when the original charges were framed.
After the evidence and arguments had concluded and the case was reserved for judgment, the omission was brought to the trial court’s attention and an application was made to add charges.
The trial court rejected the application; the High Court later directed that the additional charges be framed.
issues.conclusion: The power to add or alter a charge is broad and may be exercised before judgment, including after evidence and arguments have concluded, where relevant material supports the proposed charge. The court must act judicially and protect the accused from prejudice, using procedural safeguards where necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Section 216(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure authorizes a court to alter or add to a charge before judgment, and “add” includes adding a new charge. Sections 216(2)–(5) prescribe safeguards, including explaining the change to the accused and, where necessary, adjourning the trial or directing a new trial; Section 217 addresses recalling witnesses after a charge is altered or added. The Court relied on P Kartikalakshmi v Sri Ganesh, Anant Prakash Sinha v State of Haryana, CBI v Karimullah Osan Khan, and Jasvinder Saini v State (Govt of NCT of Delhi). The proposed charge must have a direct link to material before the court, and the power must be exercised without compromising a fair trial.

rule.if: criminal_trial and before_judgment and charge_related_material and (charge_omission or later_trial_material)

predicates.criminal_trial: The matter is being tried in a criminal court.
predicates.before_judgment: The court has not yet pronounced judgment.
predicates.charge_related_material: Material before the court has a direct connection to the factual ingredients of the proposed charge.
predicates.charge_omission: A charge was omitted despite relevant material being before the court.
predicates.later_trial_material: Relevant material supporting a charge came before the court during the proceedings.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial has not reached judgment and relevant material supports a charge, an omission or later material permits the court to add or alter the charge while protecting a fair trial.

issues.legal_issue: At the stage of deciding whether to add charges, sufficient material indicating a prima facie link to the alleged offences justifies proceeding with those charges, while the credibility and ultimate evidentiary value of the material remain matters for trial.
material_facts: Witness statements and testimony indicated that the accused demanded and received money on a promise to secure a medical job for his wife.
The complainant’s account of payment was supported by accounts from other witnesses, including witnesses described as independent.

The trial court had initially failed to consider the additional charge-sheet and later rejected the application to add charges without adequately addressing whether the alleged offences’ ingredients were supported by the record.

The High Court relied on the witness material and the additional charge-sheet to direct that the charges be added; the Supreme Court found sufficient material linked to the alleged offences and did not assess the witnesses’ credibility or the ultimate merits.
issues.conclusion: The material on record was sufficient to support the addition of the charges, and the High Court’s order did not warrant interference. The appeal was dismissed and the trial was to continue; the truth and probative value of the witness evidence remained for trial.
issues.legal_principle: For addition or alteration of a charge under Section 216 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court must find material with a direct link to the ingredients of the alleged offence and form a prima facie presumptive view; it need not decide the evidence’s credibility or probative value. At the charge stage, facts taken at face value and even strong suspicion founded on material may suffice, while proof for conviction is not required. The Court applied Onkar Nath Mishra v The State and the principles in Anant Prakash Sinha v State of Haryana and CBI v Karimullah Osan Khan.

predicates.appeal_against_additional_charge_order: A party appeals against an order directing additional charges in a criminal trial.
predicates.prima_facie_offence_link: The material, taken at face value, supports a prima facie link between the alleged conduct and the factual ingredients of the proposed offences.
predicates.supporting_witness_material: Witness accounts support the allegation underlying the proposed charges.

issues.definition: On an appeal concerning additional charges, a prima facie offence link supported by witness material means the charges may proceed to trial without the appellate court deciding the evidence’s credibility.
